sections.heading: OEM vs. Authorised Reseller on GeM: Which Category Should You Register Under?
paragraphs: Before you type a single detail into the GeM portal, you have to answer one question honestly: do you make the product, or do you sell someone else's? That single answer decides which registration path you're on: Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) or Authorised Reseller, and getting it wrong isn't a small slip-up. It can mean blocked catalogue listings, missing authorisation codes, and bids that get rejected for a paperwork mismatch you didn't even know existed.

This is one of the first branching points anyone doing GeM registration in India runs into, and a lot of first-time sellers treat it as a formality. It isn't. Your category decides what documents you'll need, how your product listings get approved, and even how much pricing control you'll have. So before you start your GeM registration, let's actually walk through what these two categories mean, how they're different, and which one fits your business.

OEM stands for Original Equipment Manufacturer. On GeM, this term applies to the business that either physically manufactures a product or genuinely owns the brand behind it. If you've built the factory, hired the workers, and put your company's name on the box, you're an OEM.

Being registered as an OEM comes with real privileges. You can list your products directly under your own catalogue, control your brand's presence on the platform, and, most importantly, authorise other sellers to resell your products. Without your permission, nobody else can legally list your branded goods on GeM. That's the whole point of the system.

There's also a middle category worth knowing: Deemed OEM. This applies to businesses that don't manufacture in-house but outsource production to a third party, then sell the finished goods under their own brand name. Think of a company that designs furniture but has it built at a contract factory. They didn't run the machines themselves, but the brand is theirs, and GeM treats them as OEMs for registration purposes.

One thing to keep in mind: registering as an OEM typically means passing GeM's Vendor Assessment, carried out by an agency like the Quality Council of India. It's not automatic. GeM wants proof that you're really capable of manufacturing what you claim to manufacture, not just claiming the title.

Now flip the picture. A reseller doesn't manufacture anything. They buy finished products from an OEM, sometimes in bulk, sometimes on a case-by-case basis, and sell those same products on GeM at a standard commercial markup.

Here's the catch, though: you can't just decide to sell someone else's branded product on GeM. You need permission, and that permission comes in the form of an authorisation code or a Letter of Authorisation (LoA) issued directly by the OEM. Without it, the portal simply won't let you pair your reseller account with that product listing. No exceptions.

For a lot of product categories, especially electronics, industrial equipment, and anything considered "Q2" under GeM's classification system, the process works like this: the OEM uploads an authorization code through their own OEM Panel, and the reseller enters that code to get matched and approved. It's a digital handshake, essentially, and it exists specifically to stop unauthorised sellers from listing knockoffs or unapproved stock under a real brand's name.

If you're planning GeM registration online as a reseller, budget time for this step. Getting an OEM to issue your authorisation code isn't instant; it depends on their internal approval process, not just yours.
Let's put this side by side, because the differences are more practical than theoretical.
Who registers under each category?
OEM: Businesses that manufacture their own products, or deemed OEMs selling outsourced goods under their own brand.
Reseller: Traders, dealers, and distributors selling products manufactured by someone else.
OEM: Sets the base price for the product across the entire platform.
